thread.title: Amazon Stock Is Down but Not Out as Strong Holiday Sales Could Drive a Rebound - Barron's

title: Amazon Stock Is Down but Not Out as Strong Holiday Sales Could Drive a Rebound - Barron's
text:
Amazon Stock Is Down but Not Out as Strong Holiday Sales Could Drive a Rebound By Jan. 11, 2019 12:13 p.m. ET Order Reprints Photograph by Andrew Gustar Text size
Early indications show Amazon.com (AMZN) had another great holiday season, and Oppenheimer is bullish ahead of the e-commerce giant’s fourth-quarter report.
Where we were: Despite tech’s fall from grace in 2018, Amazon is still up more than 26% in the past 12 months.
Where we’re headed: Oppenheimer argues that strong U.S. results should offset any international weakness.
In retrospect, 2018 may be seen as the year the FAANGs—the quintet of Facebook (FB), Apple (AAPL), Amazon, Netflix (NFLX), and Google parent Alphabet (GOOGL)—lost their edge amid a broader decline in tech stocks. Of the five, only Amazon and Netflix are in the black (and well ahead of the market) for the past 12 months. For the former, at least, Oppenheimer thinks that there’s more good news to come.
Analyst Jason Helfstein reiterated an Outperform rating and $2,020 price target on Amazon Friday. He writes that the company likely beat its domestic gross profit estimates in the fourth quarter, thanks to a strong macro holiday sales environment and ongoing market share gains.
While the holiday shopping season was a strong one overall, that hasn’t helped all retailers’ stocks, as was so dramatically illustrated earlier this week. Even traditional brick-and-mortar retailers that did well are still grappling with the shift to online shopping—and that’s where Amazon still dominates. Newsletter Sign-up
It’s not just that Amazon accounts for 44% of all U.S. e-commerce sales, as stunning as that number sounds. As consumers move more of their shopping dollars online, and increasingly use apps and mobile devices, Amazon has shown that it’s better able to convert browsers into buyers than big rivals like Walmart (WMT) and Target (TGT), Helfstein writes. “Amazon daily conversion topped Target and Walmart on brick and mortar-heavy Black Friday, with over 10% conversion, Target and Walmart recorded only 6-7%. Amazon daily conversion peaked on Cyber Monday at 11%, with Target at 9% and Walmart at 7%.”
Online sales can be a double-edge sword for traditional retailers. Both Walmart and Target have been punished in the past for not accelerating e-commerce revenue fast enough, but these sales also often carry lower margins. Add to that rising transportation costs and an environment in which free shipping is becoming more necessity than luxury, and brick-and-mortar retailers’ situation becomes even trickier.
Of course, as was true for so much of 2018, what was happening in the U.S. wasn’t necessarily mirrored overseas. For example, retail was much weaker internationally, especially in the U.K., where Brexit concerns hit stores hard—including Walgreen Boots Alliance (WBA), given Boots’ British presence —and led retail executives to say some pretty dire things .
Helfstein argues that with more sobering figures out of the U.K., even from online darlings like Asos, investors should be braced for slower international growth at Amazon. Nonetheless, the U.S. figures should help to offset this, along with strong revenue and margin trajectories at other major divisions, like Amazon Web Services.
Amazon was down 0.8% to $1,643.59 in recent trading.
